detail.body:
Split into four standalone PRs following @aoshen02's proposal: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64183, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64184, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64185, and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64186 (checkpoint-only, independent of the other three). Please review the new PRs; this original PR is retained for historical discussion and validation.

---

<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Add a default-off `CUDACheckpointExecutor` that checkpoints CUDA worker state after level-1 sleep and restores the original CUDA graphs before waking allocation tags. This reduces sleeping GPU residency at the cost of host memory and extra sleep/wake latency.

Related to #48311, which tracks this PR under Performance: reclaiming GPU-resident process state during sleep while preserving captured CUDA graphs. This PR addresses that specific optimization, rather than the full sleep/wake/drain lifecycle roadmap.

## Claims

- Dedicated workers and an external driver helper preserve original CUDA graph executables without recapture. Partial wake restores the whole CUDA state before the selected allocator tags; KV contents retain ordinary level-1 semantics.
- Driver operations run concurrently within each stage, with all-worker barriers between Lock, Checkpoint, Restore and Unlock. Incomplete responses, failed ranks and timeouts stop the executor; it never resumes service with a partially restored rank set.
- With NCCL communicator suspension, both GPU peer-to-peer and legacy shared-memory transports are accepted. NVLS, NCCL CUDA host-memory allocation and the other documented unsupported resources remain restricted. Upgrading the user-mode driver alone does not qualify them.
- The former `ProcessCheckpointExecutor` import remains an alias. Single-node tensor parallelism is accepted without a hardcoded 1/2/4 whitelist; only those sizes have been GPU-tested. The default executor is unchanged.

## Validation

Review follow-up at `42c464663cec1d9322e8664eac9c836b8a69a288`: added `Literal` typing for driver operations and reused the same ordered operation tuple. The helper protocol, CUDA calls and stage ordering are unchanged. The two unit-test files below were rerun with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=`: **129 passed, 2 warnings**, and applicable pre-commit checks passed. A separate mypy check rejects a misspelled operation and accepts the four valid operations. Exclusive-GPU tests were not rerun for this typing-only follow-up; the GPU measurements below remain tied to `c9171d7ad`.

Current results correspond to `c9171d7ad9eedd77d7633d5cdb0355018ff9b29a`, based on `9514aef85`. Four H20 GPUs, driver 580.126.09, PyTorch 2.14.0/CUDA 13, NCCL 2.30.7, FlashInfer 0.7.2, V2 model runner. The tested Python sources match the published files. Existing native components were used; this is not a clean rebuild of all optional extensions or a substitute for upstream CI.

- Helper/executor unit tests: **129 passed**. Coverage includes complete stage responses, arbitrary rank counts, failure/timeout cleanup, configuration rejection and old/new executor names.
- Opt-in GPU regression: **5 passed** — TP1/2/4 peer-to-peer and TP2/4 forced shared memory, three cycles each with Qwen3-0.6B and batch invariance. Checks cover exact output, both partial-wake orders, repeated sleep, original worker/graph identities, increased **post-wake** replay counts and zero new captures. `/dev/shm` entries were unchanged after the suite.
- Qwen3.8-27B BF16: TP2 peer-to-peer and TP4 shared memory each completed **20 cycles**, preserving original graphs and actually replaying them after wake. All four diagnostic prompts matched their immediately preceding outputs in 13/20 and 16/20 cycles respectively. TP4 ordinary sleep also matched in 16/20, but in different cycles; equal counts do not establish equal causes or exclude restoration-induced perturbation.
- Real TP2 restore OOM: one rank restored while the other failed under external GPU memory pressure; the call failed and both workers were reaped. A helper test combines a failed rank with a blocked peer and verifies bounded helper termination.

Qwen3.8-27B BF16, TP2, forced shared-memory transport; fixed first 128 GSM8K questions, five examples per question, at most 512 output tokens:

| Execution path | Before sleep | Repeat without sleep | After sleep |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Ordinary sleep | 124/128 | 124/128 | 124/128 |
| CUDA checkpoint | 124/128 | 125/128 | 124/128 |
| Corresponding full token sequences equal across paths | 128/128 | 113/128 | 128/128 |

This is a paired 128-question subset, not the full benchmark or a general determinism guarantee. Batch invariance is unsupported for this model's gated delta network attention.

A matched TP4 timing sample used Qwen3.8-27B BF16, forced legacy shared memory, four prompts × 64 output tokens, and a fixed 4 GB KV cache per GPU (1 GB = 2^30 bytes). Only the driver helper differed (serial versus concurrent stages). Both summaries use the first five cycles; steady values are medians and observed ranges from cycles 2–5, in seconds.

| Driver helper | First sleep / wake | Steady sleep (range) | Steady wake (range) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Serial | 9.601 / 4.127 | 3.396 (3.359–3.440) | 4.173 (4.110–4.298) |
| Concurrent stages | 8.282 / 1.952 | 2.132 (2.117–2.148) | 1.960 (1.948–2.063) |

These are end-to-end sleep and complete wake-sequence latencies; each wake sequence uses either one full wake call or both partial-tag calls, with the same order in both runs. They are not a breakdown of driver Restore or allocator operations. The sample supports a reduction in this configuration's wake latency; it does not establish TP8 scaling, statistical significance or unchanged inference performance. No internal time-attribution claim is made.

Reproduce the committed regression tests in a configured vLLM environment:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/executor/test_cuda_process_checkpoint.py \
  tests/v1/executor/test_process_checkpoint_executor.py -q

# Requires exclusive GPUs and a local/downloadable model.
VLLM_TEST_CUDA_PROCESS_CHECKPOINT=1 \
VLLM_TEST_MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/basic_correctness/memory/sleep_mode/test_process_checkpoint.py -q
```

The extended model and failure measurements used local harnesses, not additional committed CI tests. The GPU test is opt-in because it needs exclusive devices and driver checkpoint support. Applicable pre-commit checks were run on the changed files.

<details>
<summary>Earlier revision: capacity, serving and latency evidence</summary>

At `a2472393067b4e04e83cdb7bc3f93aa52c8a67fa`, Qwen3.8-27B BF16 TP2 allowed a separate process to allocate and write **1.3203125 GB more per GPU** after checkpoint than after ordinary sleep (two cycles on both devices; 1 GB = 2^30 bytes). This measures whole-process additional physical capacity, not exclusively graph-executable memory. This capacity measurement was not rerun for the current increment.

That revision also passed real HTTP request draining, rejection of overlapping management transitions, partial wake and matching post-wake output with insecure serialization disabled, plus awake/partial/asleep shutdown and actual restore OOM. Those broader HTTP scenarios were not all rerun for this increment. Resource-tracker cleanup warnings remain; the checked GPU suite left no new shared-memory entries. The upstream default zero-second HTTP shutdown can force-kill the tree and needs an init/reaper for orphaned children.

The earlier TP2 checkpoint steady wake median was 3.756 s versus 0.815 s for ordinary sleep with the same restricted communication recipe (five cycles, medians of cycles 2–5). These are historical end-to-end wake calls, not current parallel-driver results. Communication restrictions can also affect inference performance.

</details>

## Details

Configuration, deadlines and limitations are documented in `docs/features/sleep_mode.md`. The helper and workers must load compatible user-mode driver libraries. A driver stage has a 30-second response deadline, in addition to each Lock call's driver timeout. Shutdown terminates worker/helper processes without restoring their GPU state.

This increment also fixes a post-merge startup failure: Step5 sparse attention still imported `is_quantized_kv_cache` from `torch_utils` after it moved to `kv_cache_interface`. Importing the model registry could therefore fail even for Qwen; the corrected import was verified by the model runs above.

There is useful common ground with #62570: draining, resource preparation/restoration hooks, transition guards and failure handling. Its current prepare flow discards KV and rejects an already-sleeping engine, while this executor first offloads weights and supports partial tag wake. Shared lifecycle integration remains a maintainer discussion, not an already-implemented compatibility claim. #62570 delegates checkpointing to an external orchestrator; this PR directly invokes the CUDA driver and does not integrate CRIU or container migration. No second public checkpoint API is added here.

Earlier ai-dynamo/snapshot testing showed that newer user-mode drivers plus cuInterpose can restore multicast resources; that path also tears resources down before checkpoint and rebuilds them afterwards. Our native NVLS probes still timed out during Checkpoint on both 580 and 610, so those results do not justify removing the NVLS guard. NCCL's `ncclMemPersist` tracking also does not release NVLS allocations during communicator suspension. Likewise, PageBroker storage/operator results are not claimed as this executor's memory or latency behavior.

#56373 overlaps in process-state offload and needs consolidation with maintainers before merging overlapping integrations. #57899 destroys graphs and lazily recaptures them and remains a separate approach. TP8, actual InfiniBand, unsupported multicast resources, other driver/library combinations and full native-extension rebuilding are not established by this validation.

AI assistance (Codex and an independent reviewer) was used for implementation, validation and this description.

---

<details>
<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill.
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.
- [x] **Design Fit:** Default-off executor; existing worker hooks reused; overlapping lifecycle proposals explicitly identified.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Unit and exclusive-GPU regression, paired model evaluation and actual failure validation; CI and hardware limits stated.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Existing tests extended; compatibility import retained; applicable checks run.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Current and historical evidence separated; restrictions and unresolved integration choices stated.
</details>

+## Control request ordering
+
+The caller must serialize sleep, wake, pause, and resume operations for each
+engine, including requests from different clients. Wait for each operation to
+complete successfully before issuing the next one. With asynchronous Python
+APIs, await the operation; with HTTP APIs, wait for its successful response.
+
+`sleep(mode="wait")` waits for in-flight requests to finish and for worker sleep
+to complete before returning to the caller. This does not block EngineCore from
+handling other control requests while requests drain. Overlapping control
+operations are unsupported; the engine does not guarantee that it will reject
+them or execute them in the intended order. Coordinate multiple clients through
+a single controller or a shared lock. A timeout or disconnected client does not
+prove that the operation stopped; establish its outcome before issuing another
+control operation.
+
 ## Sleep levels
 
 Level 1 sleep will offload the model weights and discard the KV cache. The content of KV cache is forgotten. Level 1 sleep is good for sleeping and waking up the engine to run the same model again. The model weights are backed up in CPU memory. Please make sure there's enough CPU memory to store the model weights. Level 2 sleep will discard both the model weights and the KV cache (while the model's buffers are kept in CPU, like rope scaling tensors). The content of both the model weights and KV cache is forgotten. Level 2 sleep is good for sleeping and waking up the engine to run a different model or update the model, where previous model weights are not needed, e.g. RLHF weight update. Level 2 sleep is also useful when there is not enough CPU memory to back up the model weights, e.g. when a colocated trainer already uses CPU memory for offloading its own state; since nothing is backed up, restore the weights after waking up with `collective_rpc("reload_weights")`.

+# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
+# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright contributors to the vLLM project
+"""CPU lifecycle tests for the opt-in process checkpoint executor."""
+
+import multiprocessing
+import threading
+import time
+from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
+from types import SimpleNamespace
+from typing import Any
+from unittest.mock import Mock, patch
+
+import pytest
+
+from vllm.v1.executor.multiproc_executor import MultiprocExecutor
+from vllm.v1.executor.process_checkpoint_executor import ProcessCheckpointExecutor
+
+
+@pytest.fixture
+def executor():
+    calls: list[tuple[Any, ...]] = []
+    obj = ProcessCheckpointExecutor.__new__(ProcessCheckpointExecutor)
+    obj._checkpoint_lock = threading.RLock()
+    obj._checkpoint_active = False
+    obj._use_nccl_suspend = False
+    obj._checkpoint_flashinfer = False
+    obj.is_failed = False
+    obj.sleeping_tags = set()
+    obj.failure_callback = None
+    obj.workers = [SimpleNamespace(proc=SimpleNamespace(pid=p)) for p in (11, 22)]
+    obj._checkpoint = SimpleNamespace(
+        suspend=lambda pids: calls.append(("checkpoint", pids)),
+        resume=lambda: calls.append(("restore",)),
+        close=lambda: calls.append(("close",)),
+    )
+
+    def sleep(self, level=1):
+        if "weights" in self.sleeping_tags:
+            return
+        calls.append(("sleep", level))
+        self.sleeping_tags = {"weights", "kv_cache"}
+
+    def wake(self, tags=None):
+        calls.append(("wake", tags))
+        self.sleeping_tags -= set(tags) if tags else self.sleeping_tags.copy()
+
+    with (
+        patch.object(MultiprocExecutor, "sleep", sleep),
+        patch.object(MultiprocExecutor, "wake_up", wake),
+        patch.object(
+            MultiprocExecutor, "shutdown", lambda _: calls.append(("shutdown",))
+        ),
+    ):
+        yield obj, calls
+    obj._checkpoint = None
+
+
+def test_sleep_then_restore_precedes_worker_wake(executor):
+    obj, calls = executor
+    obj.sleep()
+    obj.wake_up()
+    assert calls == [
+        ("sleep", 1),
+        ("checkpoint", [11, 22]),
+        ("restore",),
+        ("wake", None),
+    ]
+
+
+def test_repeated_sleep_does_not_checkpoint_twice(executor):
+    obj, calls = executor
+    obj.sleep()
+    obj.sleep()
+    assert calls == [("sleep", 1), ("checkpoint", [11, 22])]
+
+
+def test_partial_wake_restores_process_only_once(executor):
+    obj, calls = executor
+    obj.sleep()
+    obj.wake_up(["weights"])
+    obj.wake_up(["kv_cache"])
+    assert calls.count(("restore",)) == 1
+    assert not obj.is_sleeping
+
+
+def test_invalid_tag_does_not_restore(executor):
+    obj, calls = executor
+    obj.sleep()
+    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+        obj.wake_up(["invalid"])
+    assert ("restore",) not in calls
+
+
+def test_failed_checkpoint_stops_workers_and_blocks_wake(executor):
+    obj, calls = executor
+
+    def fail(_):
+        raise RuntimeError("partial checkpoint")
+
+    obj._checkpoint.suspend = fail
+    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="partial"):
+        obj.sleep()
+    assert obj.is_failed and ("shutdown",) in calls and ("close",) in calls
+    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="failed"):
+        obj.wake_up()
+    assert not any(c[0] == "wake" for c in calls)
+
+
+def test_shutdown_does_not_restore_checkpointed_memory(executor):
+    obj, calls = executor
+    obj.sleep()
+
+    def fail():
+        raise RuntimeError("restore out of memory")
+
+    obj._checkpoint.resume = fail
+    obj.shutdown()

This remains a default-off CUDA worker-state checkpoint executor, separate from graph destruction/recapture. The current name is `CUDACheckpointExecutor`; the old import remains an alias.

The latest increment adds concurrent per-worker driver stages with all-rank barriers, bounded failure cleanup, and legacy shared-memory transport support when NCCL suspension is enabled. The description now reports the current H20 TP1/2/4 regression and 27B paired evaluation, with earlier capacity and HTTP results explicitly tied to their tested revision.

NVLS and NCCL CUDA host-memory allocation remain restricted; newer-driver/cuInterpose results do not qualify the native combined sleep/checkpoint path. #62570 is a candidate for shared lifecycle/resource hooks, but its current memory policy differs and integration is not yet implemented. #56373 also overlaps and should be consolidated with maintainers before merging. No CRIU, container migration or TP8 validation is claimed.

Current scope note: later native combined-path probes still failed with NVLS on both 580 and 610. Legacy shared-memory transport has now passed separately with NCCL suspension and NCCL CUDA host-memory allocation disabled. The historical multicast results below used cuInterpose resource teardown/reconstruction; they do not establish that a driver upgrade alone enables the default communication stack in this executor.

Historical driver investigation; these live-engine checkpoint results do not qualify this PR's combined sleep-then-checkpoint path. The later follow-up below found that the combined path still requires the communication restrictions, including with UMD 610.57.04. Current supported scope and validation are in the PR description.


Update on the driver-580 multicast restore failure documented in `sleep_mode.md`: NVIDIA has confirmed the root cause, and there is a fix boundary.

**Root cause (confirmed by NVIDIA)**

In ai-dynamo/snapshot#510, NVIDIA reported that the r580 user-mode driver (UMD) has a pre-existing bug in multicast restore (`RestoreMulticastDevices` fails with `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_DEVICE`) that should be fixed in r595 UMD and above, and that keeping the r580 kernel-mode driver (KMD) is fine. Our results on UMD 610.57.04 and 615.71.09 are consistent with that.

**Validation on a 4x H20 host (580.126.09 KMD retained, newer UMDs via LD_LIBRARY_PATH)**

Whole-process checkpoint/restore of a live vLLM engine (vllm 0.30.1rc1.dev0+g6f75cc7d5d, Qwen3.8-27B BF16) with the *default* communication stack — dispatch order FLASHINFER(trtllm)/CUSTOM/SYMM_MEM/PYNCCL, `fuse_allreduce_rms` pass enabled, NCCL NVLS (NVLink SHARP) at its default — passes 20/20 freeze/restore rounds at:

- TP2 and TP4 on UMD 610.57.04
- TP2 on UMD 615.71.09

CUDA graph identity is preserved across every round (constant capture count, zero recaptures, identical graph-exec handle sets), and per-rank GPU memory returns to within +2 MiB of baseline with no growth across rounds. So in this whole-process checkpoint setup (live engine, no sleep stage), the default multicast-carrying configuration no longer blocks checkpoint on the two >=595 UMD builds we tested. (One intermittent freeze at round 2 of a TP2 run on 610.57.04 did not reproduce on rerun; details in the linked issue comment.)

**Why the restrictive config in the docs works on 580**

Attribution from the checkpoint state files: a stock TP>=2 vLLM worker on NVSwitch-class hardware holds up to three multicast groups —

1. 98 MiB per rank from `CustomAllreduce.__init__` unconditionally calling `_init_mnnvl_buffer` (6 x 16 MiB stages + 2 MiB signal area, via `torch._symmetric_memory` rendezvous); only `disable_custom_all_reduce=True` removes it;
2. 66 MiB (TP2) / 34 MiB (TP4) per rank when `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_SYMM_MEM` is on;
3. 2 MiB per rank when `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1`.

The documented TP>=2 configuration (`disable_custom_all_reduce=True`, NVLS off, symm-mem off) eliminates all three, which is exactly why it survives the 580 defect: with zero multicast groups, the broken restore path is never exercised. Cells that leave any one of them enabled fail at round-1 restore on 580 (12/12 matrix cells).

**Implications for this PR**

- The driver-580 restrictions trace to a driver bug that NVIDIA reports as fixed in 595 and above — not a fundamental limitation. This executor's combined sleep-then-checkpoint flow has not yet been validated on a >=595 UMD, so the restrictions should stay until that is done; the multicast-related ones are the candidates to lift first.
- One operational requirement we verified twice: the host-side tooling driving the checkpoint must not stay on the 580 UMD while the worker processes run a newer one — a 580 CLI against 615 workers hangs at freeze. Both sides on 615.71.09 pass.
- Caveat: FlashInfer's `mnnvl` all-reduce backend specifically was not in our test matrix (ours used `trtllm`), so I can't claim it is covered.

The later follow-up below performed that combined sleep+checkpoint experiment; it failed with relaxed communication restrictions. The preceding results and statements describe the earlier investigation, not the current validation status.

Evidence details and matrix are in the linked issue comments; happy to share raw logs.

Follow-up on the relaxation question raised above — we have now run this executor's full sleep-then-checkpoint flow at UMD 610.57.04 (applied to both the engine processes and the checkpoint controller; KMD stays 580.126.09), 4×H20 96 GiB, Qwen3.8-27B BF16, TP2, gpu-memory-utilization 0.60, 20 rounds planned per configuration:

- **Stock restriction set (as this PR requires): PASS 20/20.** sleep median 2.95 s, wake median 3.57 s; GPU memory while asleep 4 MiB per GPU; CUDA graph captures constant at 13366 with zero recaptures and identical graph-exec handle sets across all rounds. Token-level comparison stays informational: 17/20 rounds bitwise-match, and the no-checkpoint TP2 baseline also had 3/20 differing rounds. Equal counts do not establish equal causes or exclude restoration-induced perturbation; the cause was not proved.
- **Restrictions lifted (full default communication stack: CustomAllreduce MNNVL + SYMM_MEM + NVLS), via a relaxed test variant of the executor that skips the restriction check: FAILS at round 1.** The Lock op succeeds on both ranks (~0 s), then the Checkpoint (freeze) op on rank 0 hangs past the 30 s controller deadline (control_start 07:11:38 → control_failed 07:12:08 in the executor's event log).
- **Restrictions lifted + `enable_nccl_comm_suspend` (NCCL 2.29.7; the executor's suspend/resume validation RPCs passed): same freeze hang at the same op.** NCCL suspend does not tear down the CustomAllreduce MNNVL multicast group (the 98 MiB group created unconditionally via `torch._symmetric_memory`), so freeze still runs into a live multicast object.

Conclusion for this historical experiment: the tested default multicast-carrying configuration remained unsupported at UMD 610. This is not the 580 restore-side defect (`RestoreMulticastDevices`, reported fixed in 595+) — on this shimless path the freeze/Checkpoint call itself cannot proceed while the target process holds live multicast groups (the same freeze-side hang we previously recorded on 580 with live multicast and no teardown, so this is not a 610 regression). Relaxing the restrictions by UMD version alone is therefore not viable. What lets multicast survive the cycle in the ai-dynamo/snapshot stack is cuInterpose tearing multicast down before freeze (`PrepareMulticast`) and reconstructing it at restore; a shimless executor would need an equivalent teardown step before relaxation can be revisited.

Driver version alone does not qualify the default multicast-carrying configuration. A later increment separately validates legacy shared-memory transport with NCCL suspension and NCCL CUDA host-memory allocation disabled; the current `sleep_mode.md` documents that narrower restriction set.

In general makes sense to me, but I wonder if you have benchmarked the restore time on something like TP8. Destroy/recreating CUDA contexts can sometimes be slow and the same happens during checkpoint/restore as well, and this time grows linearly with the number of CUDA contexts.

Just want to make sure you are aware of the tradeoff for this last mile of memory occupancy.

Seems like there might be some common ground with https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62570. Though the only difference is you are running cuCheckpoint directly vs we delegate it to an orchestrator. But it seems like there is some opportunity to consolidate APIs. @AlanFokCo what do you think?

@galletas1712  Thanks, I agree there is useful common ground with #62570. Sharing the engine lifecycle and resource preparation/restoration hooks would help avoid two independent sets of transition guards.

One detail to account for is the memory policy: this PR checkpoints after level-1 sleep has offloaded weights and supports partial tag wake-up. In #62570, prepare currently discards KV and rejects an already-sleeping engine. I think draining, resource hooks, state transitions and failure handling are good candidates to share, while keeping each path's memory policy and checkpoint mechanism separate; #62570 currently leaves the actual checkpoint to an external orchestrator. I would like to align on that shared layer rather than add another public checkpoint API here.

The executor has now been renamed to `CUDACheckpointExecutor`, with the old import retained as an alias; this PR does not integrate CRIU.

On the TP8 question: I do not have TP8 measurements yet. The published TP2 result is 3.756 s median steady-state wake versus 0.815 s for ordinary sleep with the same restricted communication settings. That includes more than the driver Restore call. Concurrent per-worker driver operations with barriers between stages are now implemented and GPU-tested at TP1/2/4; the latest follow-up and description cover that increment. The preceding TP2 timings are from the earlier serial revision, not the current implementation. I will keep the measured configurations and this latency tradeoff explicit.

@galletas1712 I have pushed the follow-up in c9171d7ad9eedd77d7633d5cdb0355018ff9b29a.

The executor is now `CUDACheckpointExecutor`, with the old import retained as an alias. Driver operations run concurrently across workers within each stage; all ranks still finish Lock before Checkpoint, and Restore before Unlock. The whole stage has a bounded deadline, and a failed or incomplete stage stops all workers. Actual partial restore OOM and a failed-rank/blocked-peer test both exercised the failure path.

The NCCL suspend path now accepts legacy shared-memory transport as well as GPU peer-to-peer, without requiring explicit P2P/SHM environment settings. NVLS and NCCL CUDA host-memory allocation remain restricted: separate probes failed on both 580 and 610. The earlier Dynamo/cuInterpose successes included resource teardown/reconstruction, so I have not treated a driver upgrade as sufficient to lift those restrictions.

The updated description separates this revision's five passing GPU regression cases and the 27B repeated-cycle/paired GSM8K results from the earlier capacity measurement. For the matched TP4 shared-memory sample, steady end-to-end wake fell from 4.173 s (range 4.110–4.298) to 1.960 s (1.948–2.063), using cycles 2–5 of five cycles per helper. The description includes first-cycle and sleep figures and the exact scope. TP8 remains unmeasured; this small sample is not a TP8 scaling claim or a claim of unchanged default-communication performance.

For #62570, I would still like to share the lifecycle and resource hooks while preserving the different weight/KV policies. I have not added another public checkpoint API or tried to chain the two current prepare flows. This remains a default-off experiment.
